strengths: Principled theoretical derivation: token reweighting is cast as a KL-constrained maximization of first-order loss descent, yielding a closed-form Gibbs distribution over token-level gradient utilities; this is a clean, well-motivated alternative to heuristic (entropy-based, confidence-based) reweighting schemes.

The 'one-backward' forward-mode probing trick for estimating token utilities is a non-trivial and practically useful contribution that avoids the naive O(|y|) backward-pass cost, making the method scalable to long CoT sequences.

The variance-control scaling coefficient is a sensible mechanism to prevent instability from sharply peaked reweighting distributions, and the paper provides an illustrative loss-curve ablation (Fig. 3) showing its stabilizing effect.

Reasonably broad experimental coverage: four model scales/families (Qwen3-4B/8B/32B, LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct), two domains (math, code), in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, plus downstream RL initialization experiments and easy-vs-hard task analysis (GSM8K vs MATH500).

Ablations on hyperparameter sensitivity (τ, ε) and training-set size lend some support to the robustness of the approach, and the method requires no teacher guidance, confidence thresholds, or entropy filters, unlike several baselines it discusses.
weaknesses: The headline claim that 'VCORE consistently outperforms existing token reweighting methods' is not well supported by Table 1: DFT actually beats VCORE on out-of-domain average for Qwen3-8B (37.29 vs 35.26) and Qwen3-32B (49.57 vs 45.93), sometimes by large margins, undercutting the paper's central empirical claim.

No repeated runs/seeds or variance estimates are reported for the main results; given that many gains over baselines are only a few accuracy points (and some benchmarks like AIME have only 60 examples, implying large statistical noise), the reliability and significance of the reported improvements cannot be assessed.

Per-model, per-domain hyperparameters (ε, τ·ϵ in Table 5) appear to have been selected via a grid search evaluated directly against the same test benchmarks reported in the main results, raising concerns about test-set overfitting/leakage and overstating the method's practical robustness and ease of tuning.

SFT experiments use LoRA fine-tuning (rank 8 or 64) for one epoch, while the downstream RL experiments use full-parameter training; this inconsistency is not discussed, and it is unclear whether gradient-alignment-based utility estimates behave the same way under a low-rank parameterization as under full fine-tuning, which is the more common practical setting.

The baseline 'SFT' condition catastrophically degrades LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct performance on several benchmarks (e.g., RBench 21.76→4.02, OJBench 1.29→0.86), suggesting the baseline training recipe may be poorly tuned or unstable, which makes relative comparisons to this weak baseline less informative about VCORE's true benefit.

The variance-matching derivation for α relies on a rough approximation (treating token utilities as uncorrelated with constant variance) and the paper does not clearly specify how Vq and Vu are estimated in practice (per-batch, per-sequence, etc.), limiting reproducibility of this key component.
No wall-clock/compute overhead comparison is provided for the additional backward pass on B' and |y| forward evaluations required by the probing trick, despite claims of efficiency and scalability.

The theoretical justification rests on a single-step, first-order (Taylor) approximation of SGD descent, but the method is applied repeatedly across many training steps in a non-convex, multi-step SFT regime; the paper does not discuss how well this local approximation holds over the course of training or interacts with optimizers like AdamW that are actually used.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: how to allocate supervision non-uniformly across tokens in long-CoT SFT.

The derivation of the Gibbs-form optimal reweighting distribution under a KL-constrained first-order descent objective is clean and interpretable, connecting token reweighting to an explicit optimization criterion rather than ad hoc heuristics (entropy, confidence, etc.).
The one-backward probing trick for estimating token-wise gradient utility is a reasonably efficient idea that avoids the naive O(|y|) backward-pass cost.

The experimental protocol spans multiple model families/sizes (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B/8B/32B) and both math and code domains, with in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, RL-initialization experiments, and a difficulty-stratified analysis (GSM8K vs MATH500), which shows an attempt at broad empirical coverage.
Appendices provide fairly detailed hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset curation steps, which aids reproducibility of the described pipeline.
weaknesses: The central claim that "VCORE consistently outperforms" is not well supported by the paper's own Table 1: at Qwen3-8B, VCORE ties or loses to DFT on both ID and OOD averages, and at Qwen3-32B, DFT substantially outperforms VCORE on OOD (49.57 vs 45.93) and is comparable on ID. The pattern of gains being large for weaker/smaller models but disappearing or reversing at larger scale undercuts the paper's scaling narrative and the "consistent improvement" framing used throughout.

No statistical significance testing, multiple seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere, despite several benchmarks being extremely small (AIME has only 60 problems), making single-run point differences of a few percentage points largely uninterpretable as real effects versus noise.

The per-model hyperparameters (ϵ, τ·ϵ in Table 5) appear to have been selected via a grid search evaluated directly against the same test benchmarks reported in Table 1, raising a serious concern about test-set hyperparameter tuning / selection bias that inflates the apparent advantage of VCORE over baselines, which were not tuned with comparable care.

The theoretical derivation is built around a single vanilla SGD step, yet all actual training uses AdamW with LoRA; the paper does not address how the first-order Taylor/closed-form Gibbs argument, or the variance-matching rationale for α, transfers to an adaptive, low-rank, multi-step optimization regime actually used in experiments.

The variance-control scaling coefficient α is derived under a strong simplifying assumption (token utilities uncorrelated with constant variance) that is unlikely to hold in practice, and the paper provides no empirical validation that the derived α actually achieves the intended variance-matching property during real training; it is justified mainly through a single qualitative loss-curve illustration (Figure 3) rather than systematic evidence.

The one-backward utility estimator relies on a finite-difference approximation of a directional derivative using the gradient from a single independent mini-batch B' as a proxy for the full population gradient ∇θL(θ); this introduces sampling variance that is neither quantified nor ablated (e.g., sensitivity to |B'| or to the number of probing perturbations), weakening confidence in the fidelity of the estimated token utilities.

Comparisons are limited to only two reweighting baselines (DFT, iw-SFT) and a naive random-dropout baseline, despite the paper itself citing several other entropy- or influence-based token-selection methods in Section 4.1/Related Work that are never empirically compared against.

Fine-tuning uses LoRA (rank 8 for Qwen3) rather than full fine-tuning for the main SFT experiments, which is a lower-capacity regime that may exaggerate the effect of token reweighting relative to standard full-parameter long-CoT SFT practice used by most cited production systems.

The RL-initialization experiment (Table 2) is conducted only on two benchmarks for two small models, with gains for VCORE after RL often marginal (e.g., ~1 point), which is a thin evidentiary basis for the claimed broader benefit of VCORE as an RL initializer.

The abstract/intro rhetoric ("substantial performance gains," "consistently outperforms") overstates the actual mixed empirical pattern revealed in the full results table, which could mislead readers who do not scrutinize per-model breakdowns.

strengths: Presents a principled, theoretically grounded reformulation of CoT token reweighting as a KL-constrained first-order descent maximization problem, yielding a closed-form Gibbs distribution over token-level gradient utilities rather than relying on heuristics like entropy or confidence.

Introduces an efficient 'one-backward' forward-mode probing trick to estimate per-token gradient utility with only one backward pass plus forward evaluations, making the method scalable to long CoT sequences without prohibitive per-token backward cost.

The variance-control mechanism (coefficient alpha) is well-motivated and empirically validated (Figure 3) to be necessary for stabilizing training under sharply peaked reweighting distributions, directly addressing a real failure mode.

Broad experimental coverage: four model backbones spanning 4B-32B parameters, two domains (math/code), in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, dataset-scale ablation, downstream RL initialization experiments, and an easy-vs-hard task analysis (GSM8K/MATH500).
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (data curation, prompts, hyperparameters, evaluation protocols).
weaknesses: The claim that 'VCORE consistently outperforms' is not fully supported by the per-benchmark results in Table 1: DFT is competitive or better on several settings (e.g., Qwen3-8B ID/OOD scores are essentially tied or favor DFT, Qwen3-32B OOD strongly favors DFT at 49.57 vs 45.93, and several individual code/OOD benchmarks favor DFT), so the aggregate averages mask substantial per-setting inconsistency.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported; given that many benchmarks are small (e.g., AIME with 60 items) and margins between methods are often only 1-3 points, it is hard to assess whether reported gains are reliable or within noise.

All fine-tuning is done with LoRA rather than full-parameter SFT, which is a nonstandard setting for production long-CoT SFT pipelines and raises questions about whether findings transfer to full fine-tuning, the more common regime discussed in the introduction.

The theoretical derivation, while elegant, relies on a first-order Taylor/single-SGD-step approximation and an approximate variance-matching step (using '≈' rather than exact equality), yet training is actually performed with AdamW over many steps; the tightness of the connection between the closed-form theory and the practical algorithm is not rigorously established or empirically probed (e.g., no direct validation that the utility estimator correlates with actual multi-step loss descent).

Missing empirical comparison to other cited heuristic token-weighting approaches (e.g., entropy-based methods such as Wang et al. 2025a, which is discussed in related work as a direct heuristic alternative), limiting the strength of the 'optimization vs. heuristics' argument.

Computational overhead of the probing trick (extra batch B', |y| forward passes per batch) is not clearly quantified in wall-clock or FLOPs terms, making it hard to judge the method's practical efficiency trade-off relative to baselines.
The Random baseline (uniformly dropping 80% of tokens) is a fairly weak/uninformative ablation for isolating the contribution of the optimization-derived weighting versus simple sparsification.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: uniform per-token weighting in long-CoT SFT is a real and under-addressed issue, and the paper connects this to a principled optimization view rather than pure heuristics.

The derivation of the optimal reweighting distribution as a KL-constrained maximization of first-order loss descent, yielding a closed-form Gibbs distribution, is clean and the accompanying theorem (strict improvement over uniform weighting when utilities are non-constant) is correctly proven, even if it is a fairly standard exponential-tilting argument.

The one-backward forward-mode probing trick for estimating token-level gradient utility is a genuinely useful practical contribution, reducing the naive per-token backward-pass cost to a single backward/forward pass, and computational overhead is explicitly analyzed and shown to be modest under parallelization.

The variance-control scaling coefficient is well motivated and empirically validated (Figure 3 loss-spike analysis), directly addressing an instability that would otherwise undermine the sharp Gibbs reweighting.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four model backbones (Qwen3-4B/8B/32B, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), two task domains (math, code), and both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, plus additional experiments on weaker models (Qwen3-1.7B, Mistral-7B), RL follow-up (GRPO initialization), optimizer robustness (SGD vs AdamW), hyperparameter sensitivity, and dataset-size scaling.

Honest reporting of limitations and mixed results (e.g., GSM8K degradation, cases where VCORE does not dominate), and a thoughtful discussion linking these to task difficulty and CoT supervision quality.
Additional appendix material (extended theory for Adam/AdamW, RL comparisons to GRPO/DAPO, qualitative case studies) adds depth and partially strengthens robustness claims.
weaknesses: Empirical gains are inconsistent across model scales and benchmarks: for Qwen3-8B, VCORE actually underperforms DFT on the OOD average (35.26 vs 37.29) and is roughly tied or worse on several individual benchmarks (RBench, SGPQA-1k, LCB), which weakens the central claim of a decisively superior method.

The main aggregate metric (mean of ID/OOD averages across four models) is a somewhat ad hoc summary statistic, and the reported overall margin over the best baseline (DFT) is modest (31.03 vs 29.99), especially given the offsetting losses on Qwen3-8B.

All experiments use LoRA fine-tuning (rank 8 or 64) with a single epoch on relatively small curated subsets (3.2k or 32k examples); it is unclear whether the conclusions transfer to full-parameter fine-tuning at larger scale, which is the more common practical setting for long-CoT SFT.

No repeated runs, variance/error bars, or significance testing are reported despite greedy decoding and what appear to be fairly small benchmark sizes (e.g., AIME has only 60 items), making it hard to assess whether reported differences (often only a few points) are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

The extension of the SGD-based derivation to AdamW (Appendix H) relies on a first-order local linearization of the optimizer update map around a single reference gradient, which is a substantial approximation given that AdamW/Adam maintain momentum and adaptive state accumulated over many steps; the practical fidelity of this extension is not empirically validated beyond a single small-scale SGD vs AdamW comparison.

The one-backward probing estimator's bias under finite (non-infinitesimal) perturbation scale ϵ is not quantified; only a hyperparameter sweep over ϵ and τ is shown, without directly assessing estimation accuracy of token utilities against ground truth.

The RL follow-up experiments supporting the 'better initialization for RL' claim are based on only 200 GRPO steps on a subset of BigMath for two model sizes, which is a fairly limited basis for the claim of a 'stronger foundation' for RL.
Code is not yet released and several data curation/filtering details (e.g., exact CoT correctness filtering, dataset composition) could affect exact reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is a direct consequence of standard exponential-family/KL-constrained optimization results and does not by itself constitute strong novelty; the paper's main value is empirical/algorithmic rather than theoretical.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, principled optimization-theoretic derivation (constrained maximization of first-order loss descent under a KL constraint) that yields an interpretable closed-form Gibbs weighting over tokens, distinguishing it conceptually from purely heuristic or RL-motivated reweighting baselines (DFT, iw-SFT).
The one-backward probing trick for estimating token-level gradient utility is a reasonably elegant and potentially practical engineering contribution that avoids per-token backward passes.
The variance-control scaling mechanism is a sensible and empirically validated addition (Fig. 3) that addresses a real instability problem introduced by sharply peaked reweighting.

The experimental scope is broad: multiple model families and sizes (Qwen3-4B/8B/32B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, plus extra weak models), in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, ablations on hyperparameters/dataset size/optimizer choice, and downstream RL fine-tuning experiments.
Appendices include a theoretical optimality result, an extension of the SGD-based derivation to Adam/AdamW, and a computational overhead analysis, showing an attempt at thoroughness and transparency.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ("VCORE achieves the strongest overall average performance") is driven by averaging across models/benchmarks and does not hold consistently at the per-model level: e.g., on Qwen3-8B, DFT outperforms VCORE on OOD average (37.29 vs 35.26) and is comparable or better on several individual benchmarks, and Table 4 shows VCORE starts from a lower pre-RL baseline than DFT on Qwen3-8B. The paper's narrative downplays these inconsistencies.

No variance/repeated-run statistics are reported anywhere (main table, ablations, or RL experiments) despite many benchmarks being very small (AIME n=60, OJBench n=232) and differences between methods often being only 1-3 points, which is within plausible noise for a single greedy-decoded run. This substantially weakens confidence in the comparative conclusions.

The LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct results are highly erratic: nearly all SFT-based methods (including plain SFT) catastrophically degrade OOD performance relative to the untuned Original model (e.g., RBench 21.76→~4-8, OOD average 20.18→6-9.6), suggesting an unstable or poorly tuned training recipe (LoRA rank 64, lr 2e-4, 1000 steps) rather than a property of the reweighting method itself; this calls into question whether the comparisons on this model are informative.

Training uses LoRA fine-tuning only, with very small datasets (3.2k examples/one epoch for Qwen models) and short training budgets, which is a narrow and somewhat atypical regime for "long CoT SFT"; it is unclear whether the reported gains would persist under full-parameter fine-tuning or larger/more diverse datasets, which is explicitly acknowledged as unexplored in the Limitations section.

Appendix G reveals that VCORE incurs substantial wall-clock overhead (44%-215% depending on parallelization and probing batch size) despite the main text describing the method as requiring "only one backward pass" and being "lightweight"/"efficient"; this characterization in the abstract/method section is misleading relative to the actual measured cost.

Theorem 1 (strict improvement over uniform weighting) is a standard exponential-tilting/KL-projection result and does not provide substantive new theoretical insight beyond restating that any non-degenerate Gibbs tilting improves a linearized first-order objective; it does not establish anything about actual training dynamics beyond a single greedy step, which the paper itself must later patch with ad hoc variance control.

The comparison with RL methods (GRPO, DAPo) in Appendix F is a questionable framing, since VCORE is an SFT-stage method; presenting it as outperforming full RL training conflates different compute budgets and training paradigms and overstates the contribution's significance.

The paper trains with LoRA and compares to baselines under identical but narrow hyperparameters tuned per-method via small grid search (Appendix C.2); given the sensitivity reasoning methods often show to hyperparameters, it's unclear whether baseline methods were tuned as thoroughly as VCORE, raising concerns about fairness of comparison.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely principled derivation of token reweighting: framing CoT supervision as a KL-constrained maximization of first-order loss descent, yielding a closed-form Gibbs distribution over token-level gradient utilities (Theorem 1 formally shows strict improvement over uniform weighting whenever utilities are non-constant).

The proposed one-backward probing trick is a clever and practical efficiency solution, reducing the cost of estimating all token utilities from O(|y|) backward passes to a single backward pass plus a forward pass, with a clear computational overhead analysis (Appendix G) showing the added cost is modest when |B'| << |B|.

The variance-controlled scaling coefficient is well-motivated and empirically validated (Figure 3) to prevent loss spikes/training instability under sharply peaked reweighting, addressing a genuine practical concern with aggressive token reweighting.

Experimental scope is broad: four model backbones (Qwen3-4B/8B/32B, LLaMA3.1-8B), two domains (math, code), in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation, comparisons to two recent strong SFT-reweighting baselines (DFT, iw-SFT), plus extensive ablations (hyperparameter sensitivity, dataset scale, batch size/LR robustness, optimizer choice SGD vs AdamW, weaker-model generalization, RL initialization, easy-vs-hard task degradation, and qualitative case studies).
The extension of the SGD-derived theory to AdamW (Appendix H) with an explicit Jacobian derivation adds some rigor to justify using the method with the optimizer actually used in experiments.
weaknesses: The headline claim that VCORE achieves the 'strongest overall performance' is not fully supported by Table 1: at Qwen3-8B, DFT outperforms VCORE on most benchmarks (Olympiad, LCB, RBench, SGPQA-1k) both ID and OOD; at Qwen3-32B, DFT clearly wins on OOD average (49.57 vs 45.93) and on several individual metrics (RBench-code, SGPQA-1k-code). The paper's own average-based framing partly obscures that VCORE's advantage is concentrated in weaker/smaller models (LLaMA-8B, Qwen-4B) rather than being consistent across scales, which is acknowledged only partially (Obs 2) without fully reconciling it with the 'strongest overall' claim in the abstract/intro.

No repeated runs, variance, or significance testing are reported for the main results, despite some benchmarks being quite small (AIME=60, OJBench=232) where a handful of examples can shift accuracy by several points; several reported gains between VCORE and DFT/SFT are within a plausible noise margin.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is stated as 'to be released' rather than provided, and per-model/domain hyperparameter tuning for τ and ϵ is required (Table 7), suggesting the method is less plug-and-play than claimed and its robustness to hyperparameters across new settings is unverified beyond the shown grid.

Main experiments use LoRA fine-tuning rather than full fine-tuning, which may not fully reflect behavior in the full-parameter regime typically used for CoT distillation in practice; the RL follow-up experiments use full fine-tuning but only on two model sizes with a single RL algorithm/run and limited training steps (200), constraining the generality of the 'better RL initialization' claim.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) only guarantees improvement in expected loss descent for a single first-order SGD step; it does not establish that this translates into better multi-step training dynamics or generalization, which is an empirical leap the experiments only partially substantiate given the mixed larger-model results.

The Random baseline (dropping 80% of tokens) is a fairly weak/uninformative comparison point, and its inclusion does not add much insight into why VCORE's principled weighting outperforms simpler heuristics beyond DFT and iw-SFT.
